First, we introduce a simple, scalable, geometry-aware algorithm, with explicit computational complexity and low computational overhead, that recovers a large fraction of this log- determinant contribution by selecting an appropriate partition of the data. Second, we show how to train these models using a doubly stochastic optimization framework. Finally, we investigate how sparse GP methods based on alternative conditional posterior structures can be used to learn better hyperparameters and inducing points for SVGP.

item.title: Adaptive Replay Refinement: Allocating Test-Time Compute Between Revision and Resampling
item.description: arXiv:2610.28294v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Test-time scaling allocates additional inference compute to refining existing solutions or generating new ones. This raises a fundamental question: Should I keep improving this solution, or stop working on it and try a completely new solution? Existing methods make this decision using fixed refinement schedules, self-verification judgments, or learned controllers, which can waste compute or rely on signals that may be incorrect or require additional training. We introduce Adaptive Replay Refinement (ARR), a training-free method that detects when a stationary revision reaches a fixed point and reallocates the released compute to a new independent sample; replay decoding treats the current solution as a draft and verifies unchanged tokens in parallel, enabling efficient fixed-point detection. Across seven models from five families and seven benchmarks, ARR matches majority voting on three of five mathematical reasoning benchmarks at equal compute, while reducing critical-path serial passes by up to 2.4 times. On MATH500, ARR achieves 84.6% accuracy with only 41% of the serial passes required by majority voting. These results demonstrate that detecting refinement exhaustion enables adaptive reallocation from revision to independent sampling, improving inference efficiency while highlighting the limits of self-revision. Code is available at https://github.com/AhsanBilal7/adaptive_refine.

item.title: Debiased Prior-Data Fitted Networks for Amortized Bayesian Semi-Parametric Inference
item.description: arXiv:2610.28314v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) have recently gained popularity as an end-to-end approach to amortized Bayesian inference. Yet, their statistical behavior for semi-parametric targets, such as means under missingness or causal effects, remains poorly understood. In this work, we develop theoretical foundations for debiased PFNs to perform inference on finite-dimensional targets in general semi-parametric settings. First, we show that, despite being Bayes-optimal with respect to the target, an idealized PFN can exhibit a posterior concentration rate that implicitly depends on the concentration rates of (latent) nuisance functions and can become slower as the prior becomes more diverse. Then, to speed up the target posterior concentration rates, we introduce two generic debiasing strategies based on efficient influence functions: (i) a label correction and (ii) a prior correction. Finally, we show that the debiased PFNs (i) & (ii) possess concentration rates that asymptotically match a convergence rate given by traditional frequentist bias-corrected estimators. In this way, we establish a novel connection between amortized Bayesian inference with PFNs and frequentist semi-parametric efficiency theory. Under additional assumptions, this allows us to guarantee local and global optimality of PFN-based estimators (namely, the Bernstein-von Mises property and minimax optimality, respectively). Therefore, our work provides guidelines for designing debiased PFNs for semi-parametric inference with principled and provable asymptotic guarantees.

item.title: Disclosure Begets Disclosure: A Self-Reinforcing Privacy Loop in LLM Agents with Persistent Memory
item.description: arXiv:2610.28315v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use persistent memory to personalize responses, and personal attributes in this memory pose a privacy risk if exposed. We ask how consulting memory during dialogue changes what users go on to say, and thus what the memory comes to reveal. In multi-session simulations, a simulated user with 24 personal attributes talks with a support agent that does or does not consult memory, and in both settings attributes are inferred from the full accumulated record. Across four support models, memory raises response quality but also empirical leakage, the share of attribute values correctly inferred from the record, by a margin that widens over sessions. The cause is a loop in ordinary, non-adversarial assistance. Memory-conditioned responses carry earlier values forward, often as presuppositions, and users affirm them or leave them uncorrected, so that cues and the agent's own guesses become recorded values. The loop reinforces itself, and removing the agent's mentions of an attribute lowers its later disclosure about twice as much as single-turn effects predict. Users cannot leave it on their own, since correcting a value discloses the attribute, declining to discuss it shifts later predictions toward sensitive values, and incorrect values left in place become entrenched. The loop is best weakened at the agent's response. Instructing the agent not to state or presuppose attributes brings leakage to about the no-memory level while keeping most of the quality gains, whereas filtering or anonymizing what users say or what is stored gives up much of them.

item.title: Stabilizing Filters for Graph Signal Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.28318v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generating graph signals is an important task in machine learning, and incorporating the underlying graph into a generative model enables structurally-informed distribution modeling. However, said graph is often noisy or imperfectly estimated, and structural errors can affect the generative process and the resulting signal distribution. While recent work has established stability guarantees for graph neural ordinary differential equations, the robustness of graph-aware reference dynamics, as used in topological Schr\"odinger bridge models, remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate the structural stability of continuous-time generative models whose dynamics combine a graph filter with a learned graph neural network. We first derive a Wasserstein stability bound that quantifies the effect of graph perturbations on the generated signal distributions. Informed by this analysis, we then propose a principled framework for designing graph filters that balance structural stability with induced signal smoothing. We characterize the optimal filter design and provide an explicit family of polynomial filters with provable stability guarantees. Experiments on synthetic graphs and real-world fMRI signals support our theoretical findings, illustrating the enhanced structural stability of the proposed filters while preserving generative performance.

item.title: Confessions of a Masked MDP
item.description: arXiv:2610.28360v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In reinforcement learning, one presumes the action set to be known ahead of time, and, thus, one must know if any state-action pairs are not permissible ahead of computations. In some applications, determining this action mask is the main computational bottleneck. Isolating this problem to highlight its core properties, we study how to combine the search for an optimal policy with the learning of the mask itself, under a linear MDP model in which each attempted action reveals the exact value of a linear score determining its validity. In this framework, we first construct an algorithm based on deterministic optimistic optimization and show that it is minimax optimal, which we show is also computationally efficient. However, it is sub-optimal on non-degenerate instances, as we show. We propose an alternative, which is also computationally efficient, which plans its exploration strategy. This algorithm admits a formal interpretation as an analogue of information-directed-sampling for deterministic feedback, which may be of independent interest. Finally, we study an application of this framework to transfer learning, where the invalid action set changes over time.

item.title: A Bochner Weitzenb\"ock Decomposition for Cellular Sheaf Laplacians, Curvature and Neural Sheaf Diffusion
item.description: arXiv:2610.28455v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We extend the Bochner-Weitzenb\"ock decomposition to cellular sheaf Laplacians, splitting it into a positive semidefinite term, the Bochner sheaf Laplacian, and a block diagonal term, the Forman curvature. We show that the Bochner Laplacians form a class of cellular sheaves that extends both connection and matrix-weighted Laplacians, and generalizes signed graphs to $d$ dimensions. We give a holonomy characterization of their kernel, prove the related Cheeger inequalities, and attach to them a random walk that generalizes the Gremban expansion. For the Forman term, we prove a discrete Bochner theorem, which bounds the first cohomology of a cellular sheaf with nonnegative curvature, and we read the whole decomposition as an opinion-dynamics model. We then apply this machinery to Sheaf Neural Networks, whose learnt Laplacian is otherwise unobserved. The Bochner interpretation yields a node-level conviction score that acts as an operational importance measure under frozen-model interventions, while the Forman profile provides a local descriptor of the learnt operator.

item.title: Variance Reduction with Delayed Feedback for Non-Convex Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.28510v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study variance reduction for non-convex optimization when gradient evaluations return with a delay. The server can update the parameter while earlier evaluations remain unfinished. We first analyze an ordered recursive momentum estimator for stochastic optimization. Under average smoothness and bounded variance, its oracle complexity is $O(1+\sigma^2\epsilon^{-2}+L\Delta_f(1+\sigma/\epsilon+\tau)\epsilon^{-2})$, where the target is an expected squared gradient norm of at most $\epsilon^2$ and $\tau$ bounds the feedback delay. We next study finite sums with $n$ components and obtain $O(n+L\Delta_f(\sqrt n+\min\{\tau,n-1\})\epsilon^{-2})$ evaluations. An asynchronous snapshot variant continues updating during full-gradient computations under an explicit bound on their completion time. For the stochastic method, we further replace a maximum-delay bound by a bound on the weighted amount of missing feedback.

item.title: Continual Concept Personalization in Diffusion Models via Residual-Space Adaptation
item.description: arXiv:2610.28567v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Text-to-image personalization aims to equip pretrained diffusion models with the ability to learn user-specific concepts from only a few reference images. Existing methods, however, typically train each concept independently or assume that all concepts are available simultaneously. In practical applications, concepts often arrive sequentially, requiring models to continually learn new subjects, objects, or styles while minimizing interference with previously acquired concepts. We address this continual concept personalization setting by extending residual-space adaptation to the stochastic adaptation process of pretrained diffusion models. Our work achieves the highest concept fidelity among competing continual personalization methods while maintaining near-zero forgetting. Beyond these empirical gains, the learned residual-space dynamics reveal where adaptation capacity is concentrated within the diffusion model. Restricting adaptation to the identified layers by our method preserves nearly the same performance while reducing the number of trainable parameters by up to 72\%, demonstrating that residual-space dynamics can identify the layers that contribute most to continual concept personalization and directly guide more parameter-efficient adaptation.

item.title: Two $\operatorname{ReLU}$ Layers is All You Need
item.description: arXiv:2610.28587v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove that every $\operatorname{ReLU}$ network can be exactly simulated by a $\operatorname{ReLU}$ network with two hidden layers. We present two proofs: one that is based on fillings in homological algebra and a direct combinatorial proof.

item.title: WildMAE: Structure-Aware Masked Autoencoding for Wildlife Image Reconstruction
item.description: arXiv:2610.28590v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Camera-trap imagery presents substantial variation in animal appearance, illumination, background clutter, and visual degradation. Masked autoencoders (MAEs) offer a label-free framework for modeling such data through reconstruction of randomly hidden image patches. We present WildMAE, a decoder-side extension of MAE that combines local structure-aware refinement with masked-to-visible cross-attention. A zero-gated convolutional residual path introduces a two-dimensional neighborhood prior, while gated cross-attention allows masked positions to retrieve contextual information from visible-position features without replacing the original Transformer decoder. The associated training recipe progressively introduces normalized-pixel, Sobel-edge, and perceptual objectives. In the original Snapshot Serengeti study, covering 4,744 test images at 75% masking, the reported reconstruction scores were 27.90 versus 24.33 dB PSNR, 0.840 versus 0.780 SSIM, and 0.160 versus 0.320 LPIPS for WildMAE and vanilla MAE, respectively. Additional historical records document favorable average differences under four synthetic degradation conditions and describe component variants. We present the method, experimental observations, and their scope together: the retained metrics are historical protocol-dependent results, rather than a newly reproduced, harmonized comparison or a validation of restoration from genuinely unavailable pixels. WildMAE provides a practical architectural case study for combining global token mixing with spatial and targeted contextual refinement in wildlife masked-image modeling.

item.title: Neural Implicit Energy Optimization for LiDAR Mapping
item.description: arXiv:2610.28598v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Neural implicit representations provide memory-efficient signed distance field (SDF) parameterizations for large-scale LiDAR scenes, but the geometry recovered from sparse and often noisy inputs carries jitter and artifacts. Classical geometric optimization techniques resolve such artifacts with surface energy functionals, whose minimizers correspond to smooth surfaces. Motivated by this principle, we formulate neural LiDAR mapping as the optimization of energy functionals over the parameter space of neural implicit representations. Specifically, we regularize the signed distance field with an energy functional defined on the shape operator of its level set, which represents the curvature of the surface, thus encouraging smoothness along the surface. This adapts classical geometric priors to the scale of million-point LiDAR maps. Experiments on large-scale datasets show reconstructions with improved smoothness at preserved geometric fidelity, and no additional inference-time cost. The code is publicly available at \href{https://github.com/HrishikeshVish/nieo}{https://github.com/HrishikeshVish/nieo}

item.title: Learning Adaptable Dexterous Skills via Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking
item.description: arXiv:2610.28628v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Dexterous multi-finger hands hold promise to unlock diverse skills like functional grasps, in-hand reorientation, and dynamic handover that the human-designed world assumes, yet existing learning recipes force a trade-off. Goal-reaching reinforcement learning generalizes to arbitrary object poses but, lacking any human prior, converges to unnatural and unreliable finger strategies; motion tracking reproduces human-like behavior from a single clip but cannot deviate from it. We present AdaDex, a goal-conditioned RL framework that turns a single hand-object trajectory of a few seconds---from mocap data or HOI reconstruction from in-the-wild RGB(D) video---into an adaptable dexterous skill. At the core of AdaDex is Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking: a shared policy is trained on two populations of massively parallel environments: motion tracking environments trained with dense motion tracking objective, which instill the human prior from human motion; and generalization environments with noised initial states and goals and a sparse object-success reward, which force the skill to work far off the reference. From seconds of human motion per skill, the resulting policies can learn diverse adaptable dexterous skills, such as functional grasping, object reposing, in-hand reorientation with finger gaiting, and dynamic behaviors like throw-and-catch. Our method outperforms baselines in terms of generalization and functionality, and we demonstrate transfer across simulators and to the real world. Project page: https://yuxuank.com/AdaDex/.

item.title: Simulating, Fast and Slow: Learning Policies for Black-Box Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2406.04261v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Simulators are vital in science and engineering, as they faithfully model the influence of design parameters on real-world observations. Optimizing design parameters to minimize a desired objective function is notoriously challenging since simulators are often non-differentiable black boxes. Moreover, each simulation incurs significant compute time, thus doing such optimizations naively may be prohibitively expensive. Furthermore, in experiment design settings, practitioners are typically required to solve the same optimization problem for various input distributions before proceeding to real-world experiments. Starting these related optimizations from scratch each time can be inefficient if the forward simulation model is expensive to evaluate. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a novel method for solving black-box optimization problems on various input distributions by learning a policy that guides the training of a differentiable surrogate. The surrogate's gradients are then used to optimize the simulation parameters with SGD. After training the policy, the cost for downstream optimization of problems involving black-box simulators is amortized, and we require up to $10\times$ fewer expensive simulator calls compared to baselines such as previous local surrogate-based approaches, numerical optimization, and Bayesian optimization.

item.title: Physics Inspired Neural Networks Enable Efficient Graph Coloring
item.description: arXiv:2408.01503v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Combinatorial optimization problems near algorithmic phase transitions represent a fundamental challenge for both classical algorithms and machine learning approaches. Among them, graph coloring is a prototypical constraint satisfaction problem characterized by phase transitions that fragment the solution space into distinct clusters, making the search for valid solutions challenging. Here we introduce a physics-inspired neural framework that learns to solve large-scale graph coloring instances by combining graph neural networks with statistical-mechanics principles. Our approach integrates a planting-based supervised signal, symmetry-breaking regularization, and iterative noise-annealed neural dynamics to navigate complex solution landscapes. When the number of iterations scales quadratically with graph size, the learned solver successfully tackles increasingly challenging instances, even in regimes where finding valid solutions becomes particularly difficult, demonstrating its ability to extract meaningful information from the graph structure. The model generalizes from small training graphs to instances up to 20 times larger, demonstrating that neural architectures can learn scalable algorithmic strategies that remain effective in hard connectivity regions. These results establish a general framework for learning neural solvers that operate near fundamental phase boundaries in combinatorial optimization and inference.

item.title: FiTv2: Scalable and Improved Flexible Vision Transformer for Diffusion Model
item.description: arXiv:2410.13925v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: \textit{Nature is infinitely resolution-free}. In the context of this reality, existing diffusion models, such as Diffusion Transformers, often face challenges when processing image resolutions outside of their trained domain. To address this limitation, we conceptualize images as sequences of tokens with dynamic sizes, rather than traditional methods that perceive images as fixed-resolution grids. This perspective enables a flexible training strategy that seamlessly accommodates various aspect ratios during both training and inference, thus promoting resolution generalization and eliminating biases introduced by image cropping. On this basis, we present the \textbf{Flexible Vision Transformer} (FiT), a transformer architecture specifically designed for generating images with \textit{unrestricted resolutions and aspect ratios}. We further upgrade the FiT to FiTv2 with several innovative designs, includingthe Query-Key vector normalization, the AdaLN-LoRA module, a rectified flow scheduler, and a Logit-Normal sampler. Enhanced by a meticulously adjusted network structure, FiTv2 exhibits $2\times$ convergence speed of FiT. When incorporating advanced training-free extrapolation techniques, FiTv2 demonstrates remarkable adaptability in both resolution extrapolation and diverse resolution generation. Additionally, our exploration of the scalability of the FiTv2 model reveals that larger models exhibit better computational efficiency. Furthermore, we introduce an efficient post-training strategy to adapt a pre-trained model for the high-resolution generation. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the exceptional performance of FiTv2 across a broad range of resolutions. We have released all the codes and models at https://github.com/whlzy/FiT to promote the exploration of diffusion transformer models for arbitrary-resolution image generation.

item.title: Feature Selection for Latent Factor Models
item.description: arXiv:2412.10128v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Feature selection is crucial for pinpointing relevant features in high-dimensional datasets, mitigating the 'curse of dimensionality,' and enhancing machine learning performance. Traditional feature selection methods for classification use data from all classes to select features for each class. This paper explores feature selection methods that select features for each class separately, using class models based on low-rank generative methods and introducing a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) feature selection criterion. This novel approach offers a theoretically sound guarantee of feature recovery under specific assumptions and has been demonstrated to outperform some existing feature selection methods on standard classification datasets. Additionally, it can be easily applied in a class-incremental learning setup, yielding performance comparable to that of some current methods.

item.title: Weight Space Learning for Certifiable Few-shot Transfer Learning
item.description: arXiv:2502.06970v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In contemporary deep learning, a prevalent and effective workflow for solving low-data problems is adapting powerful pre-trained foundation models (FMs) to new tasks via parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). However, while empirically effective, the resulting solutions lack generalisation guarantees to certify their accuracy - which may be required for ethical or legal reasons prior to deployment in high-importance applications. In this paper we develop a novel transfer learning approach that is designed to facilitate non-vacuous learning theoretic generalisation guarantees for downstream tasks, even in the low-shot regime. Specifically, we first use upstream tasks to train a distribution over PEFT parameters. We then learn the downstream task by a sample-and-evaluate procedure -- sampling plausible PEFTs from the trained diffusion model and selecting the one with the highest likelihood on the downstream data. Crucially, this confines our model hypothesis to a finite set of PEFT samples. In contrast to the typical continuous hypothesis spaces of neural network weights, this facilitates tighter risk certificates. We instantiate our bound and show non-trivial generalization guarantees compared to existing learning approaches which lead to vacuous bounds in the low-shot regime.

item.title: Dissecting the Impact of Model Misspecification in Data-driven Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2503.00626v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Data-driven optimization aims to translate a machine learning model into decision-making by optimizing decisions on estimated costs. Such a pipeline can be conducted by fitting a distributional model which is then plugged into the target optimization problem. While this fitting can utilize traditional methods such as maximum likelihood, a more recent approach uses estimation-optimization integration that minimizes decision error instead of estimation error. Although intuitive, the statistical benefit of the latter approach is not well understood yet is important to guide the prescriptive usage of machine learning. In this paper, we dissect the performance comparisons between these approaches in terms of the amount of model misspecification. In particular, we show how the integrated approach offers a ``universal double benefit'' on the top two dominating terms of regret when the underlying model is misspecified, while the traditional approach can be advantageous when the model is nearly well-specified. Our comparison is powered by finite-sample tail regret bounds that are derived via new higher-order expansions of regrets and the leveraging of a recent Berry-Esseen theorem.

item.title: Accelerating Optimization via Differentiable Stopping Time
item.description: arXiv:2505.22509v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Optimization is an important module of modern machine learning applications. Tremendous efforts have been made to accelerate optimization algorithms. A common formulation is achieving a lower loss at a given time. This enables a differentiable framework with respect to the algorithm hyperparameters. In contrast, its dual, minimizing the time to reach a target loss, is believed to be non-differentiable, as the time is not differentiable. As a result, it usually serves as a conceptual framework or is optimized using zeroth-order methods. To address this limitation, we propose a differentiable stopping time and theoretically justify it based on differential equations. An efficient algorithm is designed to backpropagate through it. As a result, the proposed differentiable stopping time enables a new differentiable formulation for accelerating algorithms. We further discuss its applications, such as online hyperparameter tuning and learning to optimize. Our proposed methods show superior performance in comprehensive experiments across various problems, which confirms their effectiveness.

item.title: Rethinking Generalization in Knowledge Graph Embedding: An Empirical Study and Sparse Peak Regularization
item.description: arXiv:2505.23442v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Knowledge graphs (KGs) provide structured representations of entities and relations, and underpin data management and Web applications such as search, recommendation, and question answering. Since Web-scale KGs such as Freebase and Wikidata are inherently incomplete, knowledge graph embedding (KGE) maps entities and relations into continuous vector spaces and is widely used to infer missing facts through link prediction. Despite extensive progress in KGE model design, the role of regularization has been less systematically examined, especially beyond tensor-decomposition models. The primary contribution of this paper is a comprehensive empirical study of regularization for KGE from the perspective of generalization. Across translation-based, tensor-decomposition-based, GNN-based, temporal, and multimodal KGE models, we show that overfitting is common across model families and that appropriate regularization can substantially improve both generalization and predictive performance. Motivated by these findings, we further propose Sparse Peak Regularization (SPR), a simple and model-agnostic regularizer that introduces rank-based selective sparsity into the regularization target. SPR concentrates the penalty on dominant high-energy embedding components, which contribute most to the embedding norm and overfitting risk, while leaving low-energy components unpenalized so that weak but useful signals are not unnecessarily suppressed. Experiments on eight benchmark datasets and diverse KGE models show that SPR achieves the best results in nearly all settings compared with existing regularizers such as N3, DURA, and ER. These results show that regularization deserves more systematic attention in KGE, and that selective regularization is an effective and broadly applicable strategy for improving the generalization of KGE models.

item.title: Gradient Descent on Logistic Regression: Do Large Step-Sizes Work with Data on the Sphere?
item.description: arXiv:2507.11228v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Gradient descent on logistic regression has many fascinating properties not fully captured by classical analyses. For linearly separable data, the iterates converge in direction to the maximum-margin separator regardless of how large the step size is. For non-separable data, however, cycles may occur even for step sizes below the local stability threshold of $2/\lambda^*$, where $\lambda^*$ is the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian at the solution. We ask whether requiring all examples to have equal norm is a sufficient condition for global convergence below this threshold. We prove that this is indeed true in one dimension. In higher dimensions, even equal-norm datasets can produce cycles, although global convergence holds for the population loss when the examples are uniformly distributed on the sphere. Finally, in one dimension, we relax the equal-norm assumption to an annulus condition that ensures global convergence below the stability threshold, suggesting a path towards analogous sufficient conditions in higher dimensions.

item.title: Blending data and physics for reduced-order modeling of systems with spatiotemporal chaotic dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2507.21299v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While data-driven techniques are powerful tools for reduced-order modeling of systems with chaotic dynamics, great potential remains for leveraging known physics (i.e. a full-order model (FOM)) to improve predictive capability. We develop a hybrid reduced order model (ROM), informed by both data and FOM, for evolving spatiotemporal chaotic dynamics on an invariant manifold whose coordinates are found using an autoencoder. This approach projects the vector field of the FOM onto the invariant manifold; then, this physics-derived vector field is either corrected using dynamic data, or used as a Bayesian prior that is updated with data. In both cases, the neural ordinary differential equation approach is used. We consider simulated data from the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and complex Ginzburg-Landau equations. Relative to the data-only approach, for scenarios of abundant data, scarce data, and even an incorrect FOM (i.e. erroneous parameter values), the hybrid approach yields substantially improved time-series predictions.

item.title: Optimized Weight Initialization on the Stiefel Manifold for Deep ReLU Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2509.00362v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Stable and efficient training of ReLU networks with large depth is highly sensitive to weight initialization. Improper initialization can cause permanent neuron inactivation dying ReLU and exacerbate gradient instability as network depth increases. Methods such as He, Xavier, and orthogonal initialization preserve variance or promote approximate isometry. However, they do not necessarily regulate the pre-activation mean or control activation sparsity, and their effectiveness often diminishes in very deep architectures. This work introduces a semi-orthogonal initialization specifically optimized for ReLU by solving an optimization problem on the Stiefel manifold, thereby preserving scale and calibrating the pre-activation statistics from the outset. A family of closed-form solutions and an efficient sampling scheme are derived. Theoretical analysis at initialization shows that the proposed initialization mitigates dying ReLU, slows the decay of activation variance, and alleviates gradient vanishing, thereby stabilizing signal and gradient flow in deep architectures. Empirically, across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, multiple tabular datasets, few-shot settings, and ReLU-family activations, the proposed initialization maintains stable performance as network depth increases, with particularly clear advantages in few-shot learning and large-depth settings.

item.title: Evaluating utility of clinical prediction models: A comparison of decision curve analysis and cost curves
item.description: arXiv:2509.24608v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Classification models typically predict a binary outcome and use one or more decision thresholds to produce a classification or inform a clinical decision. Decision curves and cost curves are model evaluation approaches that assess net benefit and loss across decision thresholds. In this paper we compare decision curves and cost curves, demonstrating that decision curves are closely related to a specific type of cost curve called a Brier curve. Users of both approaches set the classification threshold assuming calibrated model scores, using the relative clinical importance of correct positive and negative classifications. A given decision curve has a corresponding Brier curve such that reference lines common in each space can be included in either (e.g. the 'treat none' decision curve can be translated into an equivalent 'treat none' Brier curve). We suggest the upper envelope decision curve as a useful comparison to a model decision curve showing the maximum achievable net benefit through recalibration. We show that net benefit (used for decision curves) and Brier loss (used for Brier curves) will always choose the same model as optimal at any given threshold, but cannot be compared or aggregated across thresholds except under specific assumptions; doing so otherwise requires custom weightings.

item.title: Curriculum-Augmented GFlowNets For mRNA Sequence Generation
item.description: arXiv:2510.03811v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop an approach for the de novo synthesis of messenger RNA (mRNA) sequences encoding target proteins. This requires optimizing multiple biological objectives over large combinatorial spaces defined by synonymous codon sequences, a setting where Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods suffer from mode collapse and Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) face sparse rewards over long horizons. To address these challenges, we propose Curriculum-Augmented GFlowNets (CAGFNs), a multi-objective GFlowNet trained with an adaptive length-based curriculum driven by learning progress. In a nutshell, CAGFNs learn from progressively harder tasks corresponding to longer target proteins. We evaluate CAGFNs on CodonDesignEnv, a novel codon-level environment that preserves protein identity via dynamic action masking. Our experiments show that CAGFNs achieve competitive or stronger Pareto-front coverage and diversity while converging up to 4 times faster than non-curriculum GFlowNets, and maintaining 100% sequence uniqueness compared to RL baselines.

item.title: Wasserstein Robust Classification Error: Surrogate Loss Misalignment and Distributional Attacks
item.description: arXiv:2510.10000v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization (WDRO) provides a framework for evaluating model robustness through the worst-case expectation in the Wasserstein ball around a reference distribution. We prove that ordering hypotheses by increasing WDRO risk is equivalent to ordering them by decreasing robust accuracy if and only if the loss function is a positive multiple of the zero-one loss plus a label-dependent offset. For a class of loss functions including cross-entropy, we show that a hypothesis with perfect robust accuracy can conversely have a higher WDRO risk than another hypothesis with near zero robust accuracy. To evaluate robust accuracy directly, we develop Wasserstein distributional attacks (WDA), which add a weight generation stage after candidate support search to optimize the allocation of empirical mass under the Wasserstein constraint, rather than assigning each data point's full mass to one returned attack point as existing methods do. We further introduce a support-search algorithm for WDA that finds nearby misclassified inputs. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, WDA using our search algorithm achieves the lowest adversarial accuracy in most tested settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/OLab-Repo/WDA.

item.title: A Likely Geometry of Generative Models
item.description: arXiv:2510.26266v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The geometry of generative models serves as the basis for interpolation, model inspection, and more. Unfortunately, most generative models lack a principal notion of geometry without restrictive assumptions on either the model or the data dimension. In this paper, we construct a general geometry compatible with different metrics and probability distributions to analyze generative models that do not require additional training. We consider curves analogous to geodesics constrained to a suitable data distribution aimed at targeting high-density regions learned by generative models. We formulate this as a (pseudo)-metric and prove that this corresponds to a Newtonian system on a Riemannian manifold. We show that shortest paths in our framework can be characterized by a system of ordinary differential equations, which locally corresponds to geodesics under a suitable Riemannian metric. Numerically, we derive a novel algorithm to efficiently compute shortest paths and generalized Fr\'echet means. Quantitatively, we show that curves using our metric traverse regions of higher density than baselines across a range of models and datasets.

item.title: Specter: Fast MoE Inference via Quantization-Enabled Multi-Step Speculative Offloading
item.description: arXiv:2511.14102v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models often exceed a single accelerator's memory capacity. Offloading experts to host memory creates a severe PCIe I/O bottleneck because data-dependent routing keeps transfers on the critical path. We present Specter, an inference system that uses quantization to combine speculative decoding with expert offloading. Its lightweight quantized draft model runs efficiently on device while preserving high-fidelity expert activation patterns. This provides accurate multi-step lookahead over future expert usage, allowing the runtime to organize expert movement and execution ahead of verification and improve both communication and execution efficiency. Under single-request inference, Specter achieves an average 1.50x (up to 1.88x) speedup in time per output token (TPOT) over the state-of-the-art system. Specter makes memory-constrained, single-GPU MoE inference more practical on commodity hardware. Our code is available at https://github.com/wwwwwf/specter_asplos.

item.title: KGOT: Unified Knowledge Graph and Optimal Transport Pseudo-Labeling for Molecule-Protein Interaction Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2512.09365v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Predicting molecule-protein interactions (MPIs) is a fundamental task in computational biology, with crucial applications in drug discovery and molecular function annotation. However, existing MPI models face two major challenges. First, the scarcity of labeled molecule-protein pairs significantly limits model performance, as available datasets capture only a small fraction of biological relevant interactions. Second, most methods rely solely on molecular and protein features, ignoring broader biological context such as genes, metabolic pathways, and functional annotations that could provide essential complementary information. To address these limitations, our framework first aggregates diverse biological datasets, including molecular, protein, genes and pathway-level interactions, and then develop an optimal transport-based approach to generate high-quality pseudo-labels for unlabeled molecule-protein pairs, leveraging the underlying distribution of known interactions to guide label assignment. By treating pseudo-labeling as a mechanism for bridging disparate biological modalities, our approach enables the effective use of heterogeneous data to enhance MPI prediction. We evaluate our framework on multiple MPI datasets including virtual screening tasks and protein retrieval tasks, demonstrating substantial improvements over state-of-the-art methods in prediction accuracies and zero shot ability across unseen interactions. Beyond MPI prediction, our approach provides a new paradigm for leveraging diverse biological data sources to tackle problems traditionally constrained by single- or bi-modal learning, paving the way for future advances in computational biology and drug discovery.

item.title: Robust Residual Correction via Selective Deployment for Time Series Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2512.22428v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Post-hoc residual correction can reduce forecasting error, but always-on updates often fail to generalize: when residual signals are weak or noisy, expressive correctors can overfit and even increase the overall forecasting errors. We introduce CRC, a robust residual correction framework that couples a hybrid corrector with a validation-calibrated selective deployment rule. CRC proposes corrections via a conservative ridge "floor" plus conditional nonlinear refinement, but deploys them only when held-out evidence indicates net error reduction over a frozen baseline forecaster. CRC treats when to revise a forecast as a validation-calibrated deployment decision, not only how to fit residuals. Across standard long-sequence benchmarks and multiple backbones, CRC improves horizon-averaged MSE and MAE in most dataset-backbone pairs, with particularly large gains on complex datasets (e.g., over 20% relative MSE reduction on Traffic). We additionally report the non-degradation rate (NDR) as a stability diagnostic of harmful updates and ablate the validation-calibrated "firewall" that stabilizes MSE gains.

item.title: Efficient and Adaptable Detection of Malicious LLM Prompts via Bootstrap Aggregation
item.description: arXiv:2602.08062v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in natural language understanding. However, they remain susceptible to malicious prompts that induce unsafe or policy-violating behavior. Existing defenses in black-box moderation APIs offer limited transparency and adapt poorly to evolving threats, while white-box approaches using large LLM judges impose prohibitive computational costs and require expensive retraining for new attacks. We present BAGEL (Bootstrap AGgregated Ensemble Layer), a modular, lightweight, and incrementally updatable framework for malicious prompt detection. BAGEL employs a bootstrap aggregation and mixture-of-experts-inspired ensemble of finetuned models, each specialized on a different attack dataset. At inference, BAGEL aggregates predictions from a stochastically selected subset of ensemble members, optionally augmented by a lightweight learned router that predicts the most suitable member to include. When new attacks emerge, BAGEL updates incrementally by finetuning just a single small classifier (86M parameters) and adding it to the ensemble. We evaluate BAGEL on a held-out, source-disjoint set constructed from datasets never used for training or calibration, ensuring that performance reflects generalization to out-of-distribution attacks. In single-turn evaluation, BAGEL achieves an F1 score of 0.757 at a size equivalent to 430M parameters, improving to 0.772 when augmented with the router using fewer ensemble members (324M parameters). These results outperform popular black-box moderation APIs and most white-box baselines at lower costs. In multi-turn evaluation, BAGEL achieves an F1 score of 0.660, outperforming billion-parameter methods. Our results show ensembles of small finetuned classifiers can match or exceed the performance of billion-parameter guardrails while offering the adaptability and efficiency required for production systems.

item.title: A Jointly Efficient and Near-Optimal Algorithm for Heteroskedastic Generalized Linear Bandits with Adversarial Corruptions
item.description: arXiv:2602.10971v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider heteroskedastic generalized linear bandits (GLBs) with adversarial corruptions and propose \texttt{HCW-GLB-OMD}, a simple algorithm that combines an online mirror descent (OMD)-based estimator with Hessian-based confidence weights. Although both components are well studied, establishing guarantees for the combined algorithm requires a nontrivial analysis. We establish a corruption-robust confidence sequence using technical tools not required in prior analyses, including a weighted likelihood supermartingale and a self-bounding argument. For the regret analysis, we derive a new Hessian potential lemma to handle the interaction between adversarial corruption and adaptive confidence weighting. For self-concordant GLMs, we prove a high-probability regret bound of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\bigl( d \sqrt{\sum_t g(\tau_t) \dot\mu_{t,\star}} + d^2 g_{\max} \kappa + d(1+\kappa)(C\vee1) \bigr)$, where $\dot\mu_{t,\star}$ is the slope of $\mu$ at the optimal arm at time $t$, $g(\tau_t)$ is the observed dispersion, $g_{\max}=\max_t g(\tau_t)$, $\kappa$ is the worst-case inverse slope of $\mu$, and $C$ is the corruption budget. The algorithm attains this bound with one OMD update per round and $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ storage. We complement this guarantee with matching lower bounds for the leading $\sqrt{T}$ term and, up to $\kappa$, the $dC$ corruption term.

item.title: Covariance-Aware Transformers for Quadratic Programming and Decision Making
item.description: arXiv:2602.14506v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We explore the use of transformers for solving quadratic programs and how this capability benefits decision-making problems that involve covariance matrices. We first show that the linear attention mechanism can provably solve unconstrained QPs by tokenizing the matrix variables (e.g.~$A$ of the objective $\frac{1}{2}x^\top Ax+b^\top x$) row-by-row and emulating gradient descent iterations. Furthermore, by incorporating MLPs, a transformer block can solve (i) $\ell_1$-penalized QPs by emulating iterative soft-thresholding and (ii) $\ell_1$-constrained QPs when equipped with an additional feedback loop. Our theory motivates us to introduce Time2Decide: a generic method that enhances a time series foundation model (TSFM) by explicitly feeding the covariance matrix between the variates. We empirically find that Time2Decide uniformly outperforms the base TSFM model for the classical portfolio optimization problem that admits an $\ell_1$-constrained QP formulation. Remarkably, Time2Decide also outperforms the classical "Predict-then-Optimize (PtO)" procedure, where we first forecast the returns and then explicitly solve a constrained QP, in suitable settings. Our results demonstrate that transformers benefit from explicit use of second-order statistics, and this can enable them to effectively solve complex decision-making problems, like portfolio construction, in one forward pass.

item.title: Learning global river system hydrodynamics with a topology-informed foundation model
item.description: arXiv:2602.22293v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Accurate river prediction is essential for water, food, and energy security, yet extending it reliably from sparse in-situ gauges to the full river network remains an open challenge. Although machine learning has transformed Earth-system modelling, the same sparse and uneven observations have largely confined its advances for rivers to discrete basins rather than connected river systems. Here we introduce GraphRiverCast (GRC), a topology-informed river foundation model for reach-level prediction across the global river network. Exploiting the connectivity and energetics of rivers, it is trained on sparse gauges and predicts daily multivariate hydrodynamics with no prior river conditions. GRC outperforms strong physics-based and machine-learning models. Attribution experiments show that, compared with standard autoregressive models that rely more on temporal recurrence, GRC reconstructs river states from topology and forcing, learning the dynamics themselves and inheriting the self-correcting character of river systems. Its skill therefore barely decays with lead time, even far beyond its training horizon. It also generalises to ungauged reaches and finer-resolution networks, bringing reliable hydrodynamic prediction to poorly monitored regions. More broadly, harnessing the structure and energetics of a system offers a strategy for machine learning in other observation-limited Earth systems.

item.title: SEHFS: Structural Entropy-Guided High-Order Correlation Learning for Multi-View Multi-Label Feature Selection
item.description: arXiv:2603.03022v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In recent years, multi-view multi-label learning (MVML) has attracted extensive attention due to its close alignment to real-world scenarios. Information-theoretic methods have gained prominence for learning nonlinear correlations. However, two key challenges persist: first, features in real-world data commonly exhibit high-order structural correlations, but existing information-theoretic methods struggle to learn such correlations; second, commonly relying on heuristic optimization, information-theoretic methods are prone to converging to local optima. To address these two challenges, we propose a novel method called Structural Entropy Guided High-Order Correlation Learning for Multi-View Multi-Label Feature Selection (SEHFS). The core idea of SEHFS is to convert the feature graph into a structural-entropy-minimizing encoding tree, quantifying the information cost of high-order dependencies and thus learning high-order feature correlations beyond pairwise correlations. Specifically, features exhibiting strong high-order redundancy are grouped into a single cluster within the encoding tree, while inter-cluster feaeture correlations are minimized, thereby eliminating redundancy both within and across clusters. Furthermore, a new framework based on the fusion of information theory and matrix methods is adopted, which learns a shared semantic matrix and view-specific contribution matrices to reconstruct a global view matrix, thereby enhancing the information-theoretic method and balancing the global and local optimization. The ability of structural entropy to learn high-order correlations is theoretically established, and and both experiments on eight datasets from various domains and ablation studies demonstrate that SEHFS achieves superior performance in feature selection.

item.title: Hybrid Belief Reinforcement Learning for Efficient Coordinated Spatial Exploration
item.description: arXiv:2603.03595v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Coordinating multiple autonomous agents to explore and serve spatially heterogeneous demand requires jointly learning unknown spatial patterns and planning trajectories that maximize task performance. Pure model-based approaches provide structured uncertainty estimates but lack adaptive policy learning, while deep reinforcement learning often suffers from poor sample efficiency when spatial priors are absent. This paper presents a hybrid belief-reinforcement learning (HBRL) framework to address this gap. In the first phase, agents construct spatial beliefs using a Log-Gaussian Cox Process (LGCP) and execute information-driven trajectories guided by a Pathwise Mutual Information (PathMI) planner with multi-step lookahead. In the second phase, trajectory control is transferred to a Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) agent, warm-started through dual-channel knowledge transfer: i) belief state transfer supplies spatial uncertainty, and ii) replay buffer seeding provides demonstration trajectories generated during LGCP exploration. A variance-normalized overlap penalty enables coordinated coverage through shared belief state, permitting cooperative sensing in high-uncertainty regions while discouraging redundant coverage in well-explored areas. The framework is instantiated in two scenarios: multi-Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) wireless service provisioning, and mobility-on-demand sensing over measured New York City taxi demand. In the wireless scenario it achieves 10.8% higher cumulative reward and takes 38% fewer episodes to reach the reward level of the baselines, with ablation studies confirming that dual-channel transfer outperforms either channel alone; the taxi scenario yields consistent gains with all algorithmic components unchanged.

item.title: SCOPE: Scalable Training-Free Semantic Coreset Selection for Long-Tailed Federated Learning
item.description: arXiv:2603.12976v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scientific discovery increasingly relies on federated learning over data from high-resolution instruments, and these data are strongly non-IID and long-tailed. Coreset selection could shorten training, but existing federated coreset methods either prune with local heuristics that ignore the global class distribution, or first train a warm-up model at every client and upload class centroids of its features. This makes coreset selection a distributed bottleneck that consumes GPU time at every client, grows with the model and the number of clients, and must be repeated for every architecture. We introduce SCOPE, named for Semantic Coreset using Orthogonal Projection Embeddings, a scalable, training-free federated coreset framework for long-tailed data. Each client scores its samples once with a frozen, compact vision-language model and uploads scalar statistics per class. The server merges these into a global class profile, which lets each client remove anomalies and prune redundant samples only from classes that are locally abundant but globally common. SCOPE therefore requires no warm-up training, needs a single exchange with the server, and uploads a payload that depends only on the number of classes. On GPU nodes of an HPC cluster, with four datasets, including scientific micrographs, and six baselines, SCOPE selects its coreset up to 7.7x faster and uploads up to 293x less data than the feature-based baseline. As the number of clients grows from 10 to 500, SCOPE's time before training grows by fewer seconds than any baseline's, and at 500 clients the baselines need 1.7 to 3.6x SCOPE's time. Trained on the coreset, the global model reaches 98% of the full-data accuracy in 18 to 42% fewer global rounds than full-data training, with 8 to 21% less client computation over 200 rounds.

item.title: Variational Graph Neural Networks for Uncertainty Quantification in Inverse Problems
item.description: arXiv:2603.29515v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The increasingly wide use of deep machine learning techniques in computational mechanics has significantly accelerated simulations of problems that were considered unapproachable just a few years ago. However, in critical applications such as Digital Twins for engineering or medicine, fast responses are not enough; reliable results must also be provided. In certain cases, traditional deterministic methods may not be optimal as they do not provide a measure of confidence in their predictions or results, especially in inverse problems where the solution may not be unique or the initial data may not be entirely reliable due to the presence of noise, for instance. Classic deep neural networks also lack a clear measure to quantify the uncertainty of their predictions. In this work, we present a variational graph neural network (VGNN) architecture that integrates variational layers into its architecture to model the probability distribution of weights. Unlike computationally expensive full Bayesian networks, our approach strategically introduces variational layers exclusively in the decoder, allowing us to estimate cognitive uncertainty and statistical uncertainty at a relatively lower cost. In this work, we validate the proposed methodology in two cases of solid mechanics: the identification of the value of the elastic modulus with nonlinear distribution in a 2D elastic problem and the location and quantification of the loads applied to a 3D hyperelastic beam, in both cases using only the displacement field of each test as input data. The results show that the model not only recovers the physical parameters with high precision, but also provides confidence intervals consistent with the physics of the problem, as well as being able to locate the position of the applied load and estimate its value, giving a confidence interval for that experiment.

item.title: Binary Agreement for Efficient Unsupervised Confidence Calibration of Reasoning LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2604.19444v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reasoning language models often lack the calibrated confidence needed for reliable deployment, particularly when correctness labels are unavailable and sampling budgets are limited. We introduce Binary Agreement for Self-consistency Calibration (BASC), which uses self-consistency as an unlabeled proxy for correctness without constructing costly self-consistency targets for each calibration query. Our key observation is that agreement between an anchor response and a single independent probe is a Bernoulli observation whose conditional mean is the anchor's latent self-consistency. Pooling these observations across unlabeled queries, BASC supports both recalibrating existing confidence scores and learning more discriminative scores before recalibration, using as few as two responses per calibration query and only one at deployment. The use of binary isotonic recalibration provides a distribution-free calibration guarantee with respect to latent self-consistency. Across 5 tasks and 9 reasoning models, BASC substantially improves calibration with respect to correctness.

item.title: LightSplit: Practical Privacy-Preserving Split Learning via Orthogonal Projections (Full Version)
item.description: arXiv:2605.13265v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Split learning (SL) enables collaborative training by partitioning a neural network across clients and a central server. However, the cut-layer interface introduces a key challenge: high-dimensional activations incur substantial communication overhead while exposing representations vulnerable to reconstruction attacks. Existing approaches typically address efficiency or privacy in isolation. We propose LightSplit, which limits information exposure and reduces communication overhead via a lightweight fixed orthogonal random projection at the cut layer. Based on Shannon's information theory, this projection acts as an information bottleneck that restricts instance-specific information and suppresses exploitable per-sample signals. With low-dimensional projections sent instead of raw activations, the server operates on lifted representations without requiring changes to existing SL architectures. Adding no trainable client components, LightSplit remains lightweight and suitable for edge devices while preserving end-to-end differentiability via exact gradient propagation. As the projection is non-invertible, part of the original representation is irreversibly discarded at the client, so LightSplit reduces the information available for reconstruction. We evaluate LightSplit on seven benchmarks spanning image classification, tabular data, and language-model fine-tuning, under IID and non-IID client data. At up to 32x compression it retains at least 94% of baseline accuracy on CIFAR-10, FashionMNIST, GTSRB, and UCI HAR, 86% on CIFAR-100, and 91% on average under non-IID client data; at 8x it retains 92% of ImageNet-1k top-1 and raises GPT-2 perplexity by at most 1.15x. Against state-of-the-art reconstruction attacks LightSplit resists inversion; the strongest, co-trained attack loses up to 87.3% of its reconstruction SSIM, and subject re-identification on UCI HAR drops by more than half.

item.title: Bug or Feature$^2$: Weight Drift and Activation Sparsity
item.description: arXiv:2605.17659v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The design of modern neural architectures has converged through incremental empirical choices, yet the mechanisms governing their training dynamics remain only partially understood. We identify and analyze a negative weight drift induced by the interaction between standard losses and positively biased activation functions. We prove that under MSE or cross-entropy loss, the gradient with respect to positive pre-activations is non-negative in expectation at initialization, driving downstream weights toward negative values during early training. The drift is intrinsic to optimization rather than data, and persists across architectures and asymmetric activation functions (ReLU, GELU, SiLU). Coupled with ReLU, weight drift produces activation sparsity reaching nearly 90% in GPT-nano. We further analyze whether this natural sparsity is damaging and find that, on average, models sharply degrade above $\sim$70% activation sparsity. We then evaluate sparsity-inducing activation functions, which reveals activation spikes in intermediate transformer layers. Code is available at https://github.com/On-Point-RND/BugOrFeature.

item.title: SafeExplorer: An Unbiased Mixed-Policy Gradient for Reinforcement Learning with Recovery Interventions
item.description: arXiv:2607.08925v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Training agents directly on the task they will be deployed on often leads to the best policy performance, but training on physical robots can cause damage through falls, so minimizing training falls is critical. A standard mitigation hands control to a separate recovery policy whenever the agent leaves a designer-specified safe region. The resulting mixed-policy rollouts bias the on-policy update, and importance sampling cannot remove this bias when the recovery policy is deterministic. We propose SafeExplorer, a drop-in modification of proximal policy optimization (PPO) built on an unbiased policy-gradient estimator of the mixed-policy return. The estimator uses the score function only inside the safe region and never evaluates the recovery policy's density, so deterministic recovery policies pose no problem. On final reward, the estimator matches or outperforms truncated importance sampling, which is itself biased for that same gradient. SafeExplorer also speeds up learning near the safe-region boundary with a closed-form critic target at recovery-triggering states when dynamics and recovery are deterministic, and an imitation loss that copies recovery actions only from successful recoveries. On three simulated locomotion environments with ten seeds each, and given an already available recovery controller, SafeExplorer incurs $255\times$, $43\times$, and $21\times$ fewer training falls than standard PPO on HalfCheetah, Ant, and Unitree Go1. SafeExplorer also matches or exceeds the final reward of PPO. On Ant, where 8.7% of recovery interventions end in a fall, over $40\times$ the HalfCheetah rate, SafeExplorer reaches the success threshold on every seed and none of the five baselines reaches the threshold on any seed.

item.title: Generalized Convexity and Smoothness via Conjugate Duality, with Applications to Deep Network Training
item.description: arXiv:2608.09523v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants train deep neural networks (DNNs) effectively in practice, yet classical optimization theory does not fully explain this success: conventional analyses rest on differentiability, convexity, and smoothness, assumptions that DNN objectives routinely violate. We close this gap by generalizing convexity and smoothness, through Legendre functions and convex conjugation, into a unified optimization framework for DNN training. We introduce \(\mathcal{H}(\psi)\)-convexity and \(\mathcal{H}(\Psi)\)-smoothness, a single formalism that encompasses convex and non-convex as well as smooth and non-smooth objectives and reveals a natural duality between generalized convexity and smoothness. Building on these notions, we derive generalized gradient descent (GD) and generalized SGD via convex conjugation. We prove that generalized GD attains an optimal learning rate of exactly \(1\), and we establish rigorous gradient-energy-based convergence rates for both optimizers. We further recast DNN training as a composite optimization problem and show that its convergence hinges on jointly reducing the gradient energy and controlling the extreme eigenvalues of the structure matrix; a model capacity risk quantifies the residual error that no optimizer can remove. Experiments on six datasets (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, TREC, and SST-2) and on convolutional, residual, and Transformer architectures, with five loss functions, are consistent with the predicted training dynamics.

item.title: Marginal Calibration Masks Generator Differences in Held-Out Evaluation of Multivariate Time Series, with an Application to ERA5 Weather Sequences
item.description: arXiv:2609.33761v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generative models for multivariate time series are routinely evaluated with pooled distributional metrics computed after marginal calibration. We show that, under a held-out protocol, the calibrated Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) distance differs from a real-versus-real floor by at most the distance of the calibrated sample to the training block, so that it carries little information about the generator. We audit a three-discriminator GAN with evolutionary weight adaptation (StatD2GAN) against re-implemented RCGAN and TimeGAN baselines on ERA5 weather sequences under a pre-specified protocol: the final two calendar years are held out behind a 168 hour embargo, calibration is fitted on the training block only, and the decision rules were frozen in advance. Evidence comes from 25 matched (location, seed) pairs across five locations, tested with Holm-corrected Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. First, isotonic calibration drives KS to a median of 1.019 times a per-location noise-and-shift floor, and neither baseline is distinguishable from StatD2GAN on it. Second, the sorted-representation discriminator is the only component whose removal significantly degrades cross-variable dependence (Kendall tau MAE +0.116, Holm p = 0.002); a rank-transformed variant also degrades it, consistent with quantile supervision rather than copula matching. Third, calibration raises physical constraint violations; projection removes them, but the largest marginal change (0.0110, Lhasa) exceeds the pre-specified tolerance in three locations. Fourth, the re-implemented TimeGAN is significantly better than StatD2GAN on Kendall tau and ACF MAE, RCGAN is worse on Kendall tau MAE and constraint violations, and the pre-specified collapse criterion was not met. We recommend floor-referenced marginal evaluation, matched-pair testing, and dependence and sequence-level metrics.

item.title: Geometry-Dependent Online and Offline Approximation for Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization
item.description: arXiv:2610.00545v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study online and offline maximization of nonnegative, non-monotone DR-submodular functions over compact convex down-closed sets $K\subseteq[0,1]^d$. A supplied feasible diagonal point $\zeta {\bf 1}\in K$ gives an upper-linearizable comparison with coefficient $\underline\alpha(\zeta)=\tfrac12-(1-2\zeta)_+^2/[2(3-2\zeta)^2]$. This gives $4/9$ at $\zeta=0$ and $O(\sqrt T)$ expected online approximate regret with one gradient query and one projection per round, including stochastic gradients. The same coefficient admits $O(T^{3/4})$ regret with one noisy value query, or $O(\sqrt T)$ with two exact value queries. All objective queries lie in the cube. Our analytical offline upper bound at $\zeta=0$ improves the bound $2(e^{-1/2}-e^{-1})$ established in 2011, even with exact values and full gradients. Two constructions extend it to positive diagonal levels; one has a finite representation below $1/8$ and a piecewise rational formula above it. Online-to-batch conversion gives offline approximation and sample complexity, while a constant-objective reduction transfers the upper bound to online optimization. Both general-class coefficients equal $1/2$ for $\zeta\ge1/2$, and their deficits below this level have quadratic order. Analytic polynomial comparisons give coefficient $1/2$ for quadratics and $\max\{8/17,2\sqrt{3-4r}/(1+\sqrt{3-4r})^2\}$ for cubics, where $r=\min\{\zeta,1/2\}$, with online and offline query implementations. Finally, for discrete submodular maximization, multilinear extension and established rounding give $\underline\alpha(\zeta)-\varepsilon$ under one matroid constraint and $4/9-\varepsilon$ under a fixed number of knapsack constraints.

item.title: LLMs are Brittle to Simple Code Transformations: Introducing CETBench - A Benchmark for Code-Equivalence Checking
item.description: arXiv:2506.04019v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study how well LLMs can determine whether two programs are functionally equivalent. This is an important problem because benchmarking code equivalence helps assess LLM capability in tasks such as code rewriting and translation. To this end, we introduce CETBench - Code Equivalence with Transformations Benchmark - built from a repository of programs that may solve the same or different tasks. Each dataset instance is created by sampling a program pair and applying a random sequence of predefined code transformations, yielding either equivalent or non-equivalent pairs. Our analysis shows that even simple transformations cause a significant performance drop in state-of-the-art LLMs on code-equivalence checking. These challenges are further amplified in the cross-lingual setting when comparing programs written in different languages. To remedy this, we present a simple fine-tuning-based approach to boost LLM performance on the transformed pairs of programs. Our approach for dataset generation is generic, supporting cross-lingual equivalence checking, the generation of program pairs with varying difficulty levels, and the application of diverse transformations. In our experiments, we perform ablations over the difficulty level of original programs, as well as the kind of transformations used in generating pairs for equivalence checking. Our analysis presents deep insights into the working of LLMs for the task of code-equivalence, and points to the fact that they may still be far from what could be termed as a semantic understanding of the underlying code.

item.title: Bellman Optimality of Average-Reward Robust Markov Decision Processes with a Constant Gain
item.description: arXiv:2509.14203v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Learning and optimal control under robust Markov decision processes (MDPs) have received increasing attention, yet most existing theory, algorithms, and applications focus on finite-horizon or discounted models. Long-run average-reward formulations, while natural in many operations research and management contexts, remain underexplored. This is primarily because the dynamic programming foundations are technically challenging and only partially understood, with several fundamental questions remaining open. This paper steps toward a general framework for average-reward robust MDPs by analyzing the constant-gain setting. We study the average-reward robust control problem with possible information asymmetries between the controller and an S-rectangular adversary. Our analysis centers on the constant-gain robust Bellman equation, examining both the existence of solutions and their relationship to the optimal average reward. Specifically, we identify when solutions to the robust Bellman equation characterize the optimal average reward and stationary policies, and we provide one-sided weak communication conditions ensuring solutions' existence. These findings expand the dynamic programming theory for average-reward robust MDPs and lay a foundation for robust dynamic decision making under long-run average criteria in operational environments.

item.title: Hierarchical Semantic Tree Anchoring for CLIP-Based Class-Incremental Learning
item.description: arXiv:2511.15633v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) enables models to learn new classes continually while preserving past knowledge. Recently, vision-language models like CLIP offer transferable features via multimodal pre-training, making them well-suited for CIL. However, real-world visual and linguistic concepts are inherently hierarchical: a textual concept like "dog" subsumes fine-grained categories such as "Labrador" and "Golden Retriever," and each category is associated with corresponding images. Nevertheless, existing CLIP-based CIL methods fail to explicitly capture this inherent hierarchy, leading to feature drift of fine-grained classes during incremental updates and ultimately to catastrophic forgetting. To address this challenge, we propose HASTEN (Hierarchical Semantic Tree Anchoring), a hierarchy-aware framework that uses semantic structure to stabilize CLIP-based CIL. Rather than treating classes as isolated labels, HASTEN leverages external hierarchical knowledge as structured supervision to organize visual and textual features in hyperbolic space, helping maintain parent--child relations as new tasks arrive and mitigating feature drift. Since the shared hyperbolic mapper is updated across tasks, we further stabilize it by constraining its updates to a null space induced by prior-task features, reducing interference with previous mappings while retaining adaptability to new classes. Extensive experiments on nine benchmarks show that HASTEN consistently outperforms existing methods while reducing feature drift and catastrophic forgetting. Code is available at: https://github.com/LAMDA-CL/NeurIPS2026-HASTEN.

item.title: Magneton: Optimizing Energy Efficiency of ML Systems via Differential Energy Debugging
item.description: arXiv:2512.08365v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The training and deployment of machine learning (ML) models have become extremely energy-intensive. While existing optimization efforts focus primarily on hardware energy efficiency, a significant but overlooked source of inefficiency is software energy waste caused by poor software design. This often includes redundant or poorly designed operations that consume more energy without improving performance. These inefficiencies arise in widely used ML frameworks and applications, yet developers often lack the visibility and tools to detect and diagnose them. We propose differential energy debugging, a novel approach that leverages the observation that competing ML systems often implement similar functionality with vastly different energy consumption. Building on this insight, we design and implement Magneton, an energy profiler that compares energy consumption between similar ML systems at the operator level and automatically pinpoints code regions and configuration choices responsible for excessive energy use. Applied to 9 popular ML systems spanning LLM inference, general ML frameworks, and image generation, Magneton detects and diagnoses 16 known cases of software energy inefficiency and further discovers 8 previously unknown cases, 7 of which have been confirmed by developers.

item.title: FLEXI-Haz: Semiparametric Deep Survival Inference Beyond Proportional Hazards
item.description: arXiv:2512.10570v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Flexible survival prediction does not by itself ensure valid inference for covariate effects or subject-specific survival probabilities. We develop FLEXI-Haz, a semiparametric deep neural network model for right-censored data that combines an interpretable linear component in the log-hazard with a flexible function of time and adjustment covariates. This formulation permits nonproportional nuisance effects while retaining interpretable regression parameters. Under regularity conditions, we establish nuisance convergence rates that are minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors over composite Holder classes, together with root-n-consistent, asymptotically normal, and semiparametrically efficient estimation of the regression parameter. For adjustment covariates with finite support, we derive the explicit influence function for cumulative hazard and construct a cross-fitted one-step estimator yielding asymptotically valid pointwise confidence intervals for subject-specific survival. Simulations demonstrate reduced bias and improved coverage relative to a proportional hazards comparator under time-varying nuisance effects. An analysis of the Rotterdam breast cancer data illustrates the consequences of flexible adjustment for inference on treatment associations.

item.title: Tensor computing application programming interface: An application-oriented, lightweight API for portable high-performance tensor network computations
item.description: arXiv:2512.23917v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tensor networks (TNs) are a central computational tool in quantum science and artificial intelligence. However, the lack of a unified software interface across tensor-computing frameworks severely limits the portability of TN applications, coupling algorithmic development to specific hardware and software back ends. To address this challenge, we introduce the Tensor Computing Application Programming Interface (TCAPI)---an application-oriented, lightweight API designed to enable framework-independent, high-performance TN applications, currently specified for \texttt{C++} and \texttt{Python}. TCAPI provides well-defined type-system conventions that abstract tensor objects, together with a minimal yet expressive set of core functions for essential tensor manipulations and tensor linear-algebra operations, with operation semantics shared across language specifications. Through numerical demonstrations of representative tensor-network applications implemented in \texttt{C++} using TCAPI, we show that code written against TCAPI can be migrated seamlessly across heterogeneous hardware and software platforms while achieving performance comparable to native framework implementations. We further provide open-source implementations of TCAPI based on \textit{Cytnx} and \textit{ITensor} in \texttt{C++}, and on \textit{NumPy} in \texttt{Python}, demonstrating its practicality and ease of integration with existing tensor-computing frameworks.
