item.title: QML-PipeGuard: Detecting Channel-Substitution Attacks on Quantum Machine Learning Pipelines in Untrusted Clouds
item.description: arXiv:2605.25066v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As machine-learning workloads move onto quantum hardware they inherit a trust problem classical AI deployments have largely solved and quantum ones have not: quantum machine learning (QML) is already sold as a cloud service, and a customer cannot check that the circuit they paid for is actually the circuit that ran. We show the gap is exploitable. A malicious or cost-cutting provider can substitute the declared quantum channel with one that reproduces every accuracy test the customer performs, passes the single-observable checks used in practice, and still differs from the declared computation at the channel level. We call this a channel-substitution attack and instantiate it in three deployments: audit evasion, service downgrade, and result forgery in reproducibility review. QML-PipeGuard detects the attack at runtime from measurement statistics the customer already collects. Its guarantee is two-sided, stated in the distance a local verifier measures: any substitution shifting a single-qubit output marginal by $\delta$ in trace norm forces a contract deviation of at least $\delta/\sqrt{3}$, the constant tight and independent of qubit count; the guarantee is relative to the chosen observable family and reference-input set. For local-unitary substitutions the adversary's blind set is characterised exactly, as a commutation condition, which gives the defender a rule for choosing challenge inputs that shrinks it. A finite-shot budget rule bounds false accepts and false alarms at once, one tolerance separates attack from the benign drift observed here, and every decision enters a hash-anchored audit trail. On an IBM Heron r2 processor a substituted quantum-kernel intrusion-detection pipeline evades the weak contract and our verifier halts it, while the honest channel stays within tolerance.

item.title: $H^2(\Omega)$ A Priori Error Bounds for Boundary-Adapted PINNs Solving Elliptic Dirichlet Problems
item.description: arXiv:2607.19167v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the numerical resolution of uniformly elliptic Dirichlet boundary value problems (BVPs) by minimization of the PDE residual over a hypothesis space of Neural Networks made to satisfy exactly the boundary conditions through multiplication by a user-defined \emph{distance-to-boundary approximation} $\rho$. While an $L^2(\partial\Omega)$ boundary penalty cannot generally guarantee $H^2(\Omega)$ error control, we show that exact enforcement can, provided $\rho$ is chosen appropriately. More precisely, we identify a sharp sufficient condition on $\rho$ preserving the regularity needed for $H^2(\Omega)$ error control, provide practical constructions of such $\rho$ for general smooth domains $\Omega$, and refer to the resulting networks as \emph{boundary-adapted}. For boundary-adapted Rectified Quadratic Unit (ReQU) and hyperbolic tangent (tanh) networks, we then derive explicit high-probability $H^2(\Omega)$ convergence rates by combining approximation-theoretic and statistical-learning arguments, making explicit the dependence on $\rho$. Numerical experiments support our theoretical results, showing that appropriate choices of $\rho$ improve accuracy and convergence, while poorly chosen distance functions can substantially degrade the solution. Our proof also yields new VC-dimension bounds for hypothesis spaces of higher-order derivatives of ReQU and tanh networks, together with new approximation bounds for shallow ReQU networks in higher-order Sobolev norms, all of which are of important independent interest.

item.title: CFR without Unbiasedness: Debit-Budgeted Public Feedback
item.description: arXiv:2608.14761v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: At a finite public-chance cut, partial counterfactual regret minimization (CFR) can evaluate successive outcome batches at learner states changed by earlier batches. Balanced coverage then lacks the conditional unbiasedness used by Monte Carlo CFR analyses. We introduce \emph{target debit}, the one-sided cumulative underestimation needed to transfer regret on delivered feedback to the dense target game. Our central theorem bounds weighted exploitability by delivered-row regret, target debit, and a native alternating-update correction. This yields Debit-Budgeted CFR (DB-CFR), which selects a public plan from completed history, executes it once, and settles its debit afterward. Complete coverage has zero debit and supplies exact recovery. With at most $\ell$ unsettled blocks, hidden debit is bounded by the sum of the $\ell$ largest predictable block envelopes; for fixed $\ell$ and polynomial output weights, the resulting $O(T^{-1})$ term preserves the additive-RM/RM+ rate. A finite converse gives equal-metadata plans with charges $0$ and $11/8$, proving that a nontrivial strict-budget decision requires semantic information or bounded post-execution settlement. In two released heads-up no-limit hold'em turn endgames, all 42 registered shallow comparisons favor partial coverage before complete coverage overtakes it between 32 and 64 rounds. In public Leduc, a lagged rule fixed on four development orders beats the best matched-recurrence-work fixed width on all ten unseen orders (median NashConv gain $0.0456$) without future candidate replay.

item.title: The surprising simplicity of forecasting quantum chaotic many-body dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.10697v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurately simulating chaotic quantum many-body dynamics remains a major computational challenge for classical methods, due to the rapid buildup and spatial spreading of entanglement during the evolution. This raises the question of whether machine learning can provide an effective alternative for predicting quantum dynamics. We address this question by formulating quantum dynamics as a time-series forecasting problem, using a few-qubit PXP chain, realizable with Rydberg-atom arrays, as a benchmark. By varying the initial state, the system spans dynamical regimes ranging from ergodic behavior to quantum many-body scarring, providing a controlled setting for testing forecasting models across qualitatively different dynamics. We compare two contrasting architectures: an expressive nonlinear Transformer and DLinear, a simple linear forecasting model. The Transformer accurately predicts dynamics in the more ergodic regime, but its performance progressively deteriorates as the initial state approaches the scarred limit. In contrast, DLinear remains accurate across the entire family of initial states, with its main deviations consisting of small high-frequency oscillations that have little effect on the overall prediction error. Remarkably, these results show that observables generated by complex quantum many-body dynamics can be forecast with high accuracy through a simple linear mapping from past to future observations. This reveals that the complexity of the underlying quantum evolution need not translate into an equally complex forecasting problem.

item.title: TTS-Q: Speaker-Aware Post-Training Quantization of Text-to-Speech Diffusion Transformers
item.description: arXiv:2610.12474v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) can clone a voice from seconds of audio. Yet the quality comes from billion-parameter diffusion transformers whose size and multi-step sampling put them out of reach of the on-device, assistive, and real-time applications that need them most. Post-training quantization (PTQ) shrinks such models without retraining, but it has been built for language and vision, not speech. At 4 bits, a strong quantizer leaves intelligibility close to full precision but consistently erodes speaker timbre, so error rates stay low while the voice drifts from the target speaker. We ask why quantization hurts speech, where the damage lives, and whether it can be repaired without retraining. To find out, we run the first 4-bit weight-and-activation (W4A4) PTQ study of a TTS diffusion transformer at 1B and 3.5B. The timbre cost comes from both the weight and the activation quantization, but only the activation part has the timestep structure a precision schedule can exploit. We therefore introduce TTS-Q, which selects hard-to-quantize items from task-matched calibration candidates and applies a budget-balanced mixed-precision schedule that assigns higher precision to late-step feed-forward activations. TTS-Q recovers timbre best at both scales, at no cost to intelligibility. Separately, the deployed calibrated-W4A4 reference reduces peak memory on GPU, providing a practical reference for resource-constrained TTS deployment.

item.title: LLM-Attack Suite: A Unified Red-Team Framework for Privacy Evaluation of Split and Distributed LLM Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.22722v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Split language models keep input text on a client but send intermediate representations to a server. Attacks can reconstruct text from these messages. Comparing privacy evaluations is difficult when attackers see different messages, know different model weights or use different datasets and recovery measures. We present LLM-Attack Suite, a framework that records these choices and lets researchers check, compare and extend an evaluation. Compatible attacks reuse recorded messages, and their predictions are saved for independent scoring. The scoring rule requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass. Reports also identify attacks that remain untested. In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding gradients returned during training increased token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%. The 95% interval for the token gain lay above the two-percentage-point threshold fixed before testing. This experiment is shared with a companion study; here it tests how the evaluation responds to a change in attacker access. Further studies measure how corpus choice and compression defences affect recovery, compare an adapted published attack with its reference implementation, and test the measurement code. The framework reports implementation checks separately from measured attack effectiveness. Each privacy claim should state the attacker, dataset and scoring rule, report its controls and identify untested attacks.
